site: Diagnostic privacy layer (diagnostics.py), affecting every site's account/login/submission failure evidence -- seen on Chipotle's Workday Create Account form
class: A privacy sanitizer could not distinguish a value the user typed from a message the site itself displayed, so it erased both identically -- destroying the one thing needed to explain a failure, across six attempts spanning four days
symptom: Chipotle's Workday account-creation form stayed open on every attempt from 9 through 12 October, and every single piece of evidence the agent kept about it was unreadable: logs/ui_run_*.log was wall-to-wall 'RUNTIME: private details omitted' (even the category name was wrong -- ACCOUNT_HELD, LOGIN_FAILED, FORM_ERROR and dozens of other real categories were not in diagnostics.LOG_OPERATIONS and fell through to the generic 'RUNTIME'), and the forensic account/*.txt snapshot held every accessible-tree label to the same 25-word field-label allow-list, so a genuine Workday error banner (role=alert) would read identically to every ordinary redacted field. No human or agent reviewing the run's evidence could tell why it failed.
root_cause: diagnostics.sanitize_log_line collapsed every log line to its bare category plus 'private details omitted', with no distinction between a category whose message is a value the user typed (FIELD_COMMITTED, CODE, PASSCODE) and one whose message is the site's own text or the agent's own stated reason for stopping (ACCOUNT_CREATE_FAILED, LOGIN_REJECTED, FORM_ERROR). Separately, diagnostics.LOG_OPERATIONS had not been kept in sync with the categories actually used across the codebase, so most failure-signalling categories silently became 'RUNTIME' instead of keeping even their own name. diagnostics.sanitize_snapshot and sanitize_dom held every element's text, including role=alert/status banners, to the same exact-match SAFE_LABELS allow-list used for ordinary form-field labels, with no carve-out for text that is structurally the site speaking to the user rather than a value anyone entered.
why_tests_missed: tests/test_diagnostic_sanitization.py only asserted that secrets and PII sentinels never survived sanitization -- it never asserted the reverse, that a non-secret, site-authored error or status message *should* survive. No test compared diagnostics.LOG_OPERATIONS against the categories real logger.* calls in the codebase actually emit, so the drift between them had no regression coverage at all.
fix: Added CONTENT_PRESERVING_OPERATIONS, a reviewed subset of LOG_OPERATIONS (account/login/submission/handoff failure categories, each verified call-site by call-site to interpolate only a static reason string, a hostname, or a value sanitize_text already strips) whose message now survives sanitize_text's secret/PII scrubbing instead of being discarded outright. Synced LOG_OPERATIONS to the full set of categories actually used by logger.* calls across the codebase, so a category is never silently genericized to RUNTIME. Added STATUS_ROLES (alert, status) to sanitize_snapshot and sanitize_dom: text under those roles now keeps its sanitize_text'd content instead of being held to the field-label allow-list, since that text is the site's own message, never a typed value. Every other category and role keeps the prior fully-opaque behaviour.
prevention: A privacy sanitizer needs two allow-lists, not one: what a human/agent typed (always redact) and what the system being automated displayed back (safe to keep, after the same secret/PII scrubbing everything else gets). Collapsing both into a single 'omit unless exactly recognized' rule is safe by default but makes every failure on that code path permanently undebuggable, not just temporarily inconvenient. When a sanitizer's allow-list is a fixed set of category names or labels, add a test that diffs it against what the codebase actually emits -- an allow-list that silently drifts out of sync fails exactly the same way an entry removed on purpose would, with no signal that it happened.
